pos: n. and v. (the cutting of wool from sheep; a season of feasting in Israel, the scene of two bloody episodes, and the silence of Isaiah's Lamb)
etymology: From Old English sceran, to cut or shear. The Hebrew at 1 Samuel 25:2 is gazaz, to shear or cut off; the “shearing house” of 2 Kings 10:12 is beth eqed ha-roim, literally the binding-house of the shepherds.
biblical_def: Sheepshearing in Israel was a harvest and a festival, which is what gives its two grim appearances their force. Nabal was “shearing his sheep in Carmel” (1 Samuel 25:2) when David's young men came asking for provision, and his refusal at the height of his plenty nearly cost every male in his household their lives — Abigail's intervention is one of the great pictures of a mediator standing between wrath and the guilty. The second is worse. Jehu, riding to Samaria, met the brethren of Ahaziah “at the shearing house in the way” (2 Kings 10:12), and “slew them at the pit of the shearing house, even two and forty men” (2 Kings 10:14). A place of festival became a place of slaughter. Isaiah takes the ordinary scene of a shearing pen and makes it the image of the Servant's silence: “as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). The comparison is precise and terrible — not the roar of a beast fighting, but the settled stillness of an animal handled by men, and the Philippian eunuch was reading exactly this verse when Philip preached Jesus unto him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shearing as the act of clipping with shears, particularly the cutting off of wool from sheep, and also the wool of one season.
webster_full: SHEARING, ppr. Cutting off with shears; clipping.
SHEARING, n. The act or operation of clipping or cutting off with shears, as the wool from sheep.
2. The wool cut off from sheep at one time.
SHEAR, v.t. To cut or clip something from the surface with an instrument of two blades; to separate any thing from the surface by shears.
SHEARER, n. One that shears sheep.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 25:2
And there was a man in Maon, whose possessions were in Carmel; and the man was very great, and he had three thousand sheep, and a thousand goats: and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel.
2 Kings 10:14
And he said, Take them alive. And they took them alive, and slew them at the pit of the shearing house, even two and forty men; neither left he any of them.
Isaiah 53:7
He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.
Acts 8:32
The place of the scripture which he read was this, He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth:
corruption_summary: Isaiah 53 is reassigned to the nation or to an unnamed sufferer, and the silence before the shearers is emptied of its substitutionary meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: The prevailing critical reading takes the Servant of Isaiah 53 as a personification of Israel rather than an individual, or as an anonymous righteous sufferer of the prophet's own day. Neither reading survives the chapter's own grammar, in which the Servant suffers for the people who confess all we like sheep have gone astray — the Servant and the flock cannot be the same party. Acts 8 settles the matter for the church: the eunuch asked whether the prophet spoke of himself or of some other man, and Philip, beginning at the same scripture, preached unto him Jesus. That is the apostolic exegesis, given in the text.

The image itself deserves attention and is often skipped. A sheep at shearing is not being killed; it is being handled, held down, and stripped, and it does not resist. Isaiah chose an ordinary and unbloody scene to describe the demeanour of Christ under examination — before Pilate He answered nothing, and the governor marvelled. The silence was not stoicism and not helplessness. He had legions at command and did not call them. What looked like a beast in the hands of shearers was the deliberate self-offering of the Lamb, and the same chapter says it pleased the LORD to bruise Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew gazaz, to shear — 1 Samuel 25:2; beth eqed ha-roim, the shepherds' binding house — 2 Kings 10:12; gozez, a shearer — Isaiah 53:7; Greek keiro, to shear — Acts 8:32.
roots_lines: Hebrew gazaz — to shear, cut off; 1 Samuel 25:2 and Genesis 38:12.
Hebrew beth eqed — a binding house; the “shearing house” where Jehu met Ahaziah's brethren.
Hebrew gozez — one who shears; the participle in Isaiah 53:7.
Greek keiro — to shear or cut hair; Acts 8:32, quoting Isaiah in the Greek.
Hebrew alam — to be dumb, bound to silence; the verb of the Servant's stillness.
usage: “He was shearing his sheep in Carmel” — Nabal's plenty, and his refusal.
“The pit of the shearing house” — a place of festival turned to slaughter.
“As a sheep before her shearers is dumb” — handled, stripped, and silent.

pos: n. pl. (workmen who drive oakum into a ship's seams to make her watertight; twice in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, in the roll of her tradesmen)
etymology: From Latin calcare, to tread or press in, through Old French cauquer. The Hebrew phrase at Ezekiel 27:9 is machaziqe bidqek, literally “the strengtheners of thy breach” — those who close the gaps.
biblical_def: Ezekiel's lament over Tyre is one of the most detailed catalogues of ancient commerce in any literature, and the calkers stand in it: “The ancients of Gebal and the wise men thereof were in thee thy calkers: all the ships of the sea with their mariners were in thee to occupy thy merchandise” (Ezekiel 27:9). The Hebrew names them by their work — the strengtheners of the breach, the men who drove fibre into the seams so that the sea stayed outside. Tyre had hired the finest, the elders and wise men of Gebal, and she was still a city that would sink. The second occurrence puts them in the inventory of the loss: “thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise… shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin” (Ezekiel 27:27). The prophet's point is stated at the head of the chapter in Tyre's own boast: “O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty” (Ezekiel 27:3). A perfectly built ship, perfectly sealed by the best workmen in the world, going down — that is the figure, and it is aimed at pride and not at shipwrights.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines calk as to drive oakum or old ropes into the seams of a ship to prevent leaking, and a calker as the man who does it.
webster_full: CALKER, n. One who calks ships; formerly, an officer in the port of London, who inspected vessels.
CALK, v.t. To drive oakum or old ropes untwisted, into the seams of a ship, to prevent their leaking, or admitting water.
CALKING, ppr. Driving oakum into the seams of a ship, to prevent leaking.
OAKUM, n. The substance of old ropes untwisted and pulled into loose hemp; used for calking the seams of ships.
SEAM, n. In ships, the joint of two planks.
scriptures: Ezekiel 27:9
The ancients of Gebal and the wise men thereof were in thee thy calkers: all the ships of the sea with their mariners were in thee to occupy thy merchandise.
Ezekiel 27:27

Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise, and all thy men of war, that are in thee, and in all thy company which is in the midst of thee, shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin.
Ezekiel 27:3
And say unto Tyrus, O thou that art situate at the entry of the sea, which art a merchant of the people for many isles, Thus saith the Lord GOD; O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty.
Ezekiel 28:2

Son of man, say unto the prince of Tyrus, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet thou art a man, and not God, though thou set thine heart as the heart of God:
corruption_summary: Ezekiel 27 is read as an economic elegy without a verdict, when the prophet's whole argument is that the finest workmanship cannot save a proud city.
corruption_paragraphs: Commentators frequently admire Ezekiel 27 as a window into Iron Age Mediterranean trade — which it is — and stop there, treating the chapter as an antiquarian catalogue with a mournful tone. The catalogue is an argument. Every item in the list is an excellence: the best fir, the best cedar, the best oaks, the best linen, elders of Gebal as calkers, princes of Zidon as mariners. Ezekiel is building the finest ship in the world so that the reader watches it go down, and the next chapter names the reason without ambiguity: because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God. Skill is not the target; the boast is.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the standing of competence before God. There is nothing here against craftsmanship — Scripture praises Bezaleel by name and fills him with the Spirit of God for skilled work — and nothing against commerce, which the same chapter describes without disdain. What sinks Tyre is that her excellence became her confession of faith. A civilisation, a company, or a church may be manned by wise men from Gebal and still be a vessel whose seams are the least of its problems.
roots_summary: Hebrew machaziqe bidqek, strengtheners of thy breach — Ezekiel 27:9; bedeq, a fissure or breach; chazaq, to make strong; Latin calcare, to press in.
roots_lines: Hebrew bedeq — a breach, fissure, the gap in a structure; the word behind “calkers.”
Hebrew chazaq — to be strong, to repair; the participle gives “strengtheners of the breach.”
Hebrew Gebal — the Phoenician port the Greeks called Byblos, famed for its craftsmen.
Hebrew oniyyah — a ship; the vessels of Ezekiel's figure.
Latin calcare, to tread or press — the root of English calk.
usage: “The ancients of Gebal… were in thee thy calkers” — the best men in the world at closing seams.
“Shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin” — the crew inventoried in the loss.
“I am of perfect beauty” — the boast the whole chapter is built to answer.

pos: n. (the iron blade fixed before a ploughshare to cut the sod; named among the tools Israel had to carry to the Philistines to be sharpened)
etymology: From Latin culter, a knife or ploughshare, through Old English culter. The Hebrew at 1 Samuel 13:20 is et, a ploughshare or mattock — the same word Isaiah and Micah use for what swords shall be beaten into.
biblical_def: The coulter appears in one of the most humiliating passages in Israel's history. “But all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock” (1 Samuel 13:20). The verse before explains why: “Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears” (1 Samuel 13:19). A nation without metalworkers cannot arm itself, and it cannot even farm without asking permission of its occupiers. The consequence is stated in the day of battle: “there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people that were with Saul and Jonathan” (1 Samuel 13:22). Two men in the army had weapons. It is against exactly this background that Jonathan and his armourbearer climb the rock at Michmash on the confession that “there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few”. The coulter is thus a small iron detail that measures a great disarmament, and the chapter is arranged so that the victory which follows can be credited to nobody but God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines coulter as the fore iron of a plough, with a sharp edge, that cuts the earth or sod.
webster_full: COULTER, n. The fore iron of a plow, with a sharp edge for cutting the earth or sod.
PLOWSHARE, n. The share, or iron that cuts the ground at the bottom of the furrow, and raises the slice to the mold board.
MATTOCK, n. A tool to grub up weeds or roots; a pickax.
SMITH, n. Literally, the striker, the beater; hence, one who works in metals.
SHARPEN, v.t. To make sharp; to give a keen edge or fine point to.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 13:20
But all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock.
1 Samuel 13:19
Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears:
1 Samuel 13:22

So it came to pass in the day of battle, that there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people that were with Saul and Jonathan: but with Saul and with Jonathan his son was there found.
1 Samuel 14:6

And Jonathan said to the young man that bare his armour, Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.
corruption_summary: The detail is skipped as agricultural trivia, and the deliberate structure that credits the victory to God alone is missed with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Readers hurry past 1 Samuel 13:19-22 because it reads like an inventory of farm tools, and in doing so they lose the frame the narrator built for the next chapter. The historian is establishing, item by item, that Israel could not have won: no smith in the land, no forge, every plough blade sharpened at the enemy's price, and in the day of battle two swords in the whole army. This is the same literary strategy by which Gideon's army was cut from thirty-two thousand to three hundred, and it exists for the reason God gave Gideon — lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the loss is one of attentive reading. The principle to recover is that Scripture's small material details are usually load-bearing. A coulter is not a symbol, and the passage is not allegory; it is a plain record of an occupied people paying for the sharpening of their own ploughs. But the narrator has selected it, and the selection makes an argument about who wins battles. Jonathan states the doctrine in the next chapter in as many words, and the whole tool inventory is there so that his sentence lands with weight.
roots_summary: Hebrew et, a ploughshare or coulter — 1 Samuel 13:20; charash, a craftsman or smith — 1 Samuel 13:19; Latin culter, a knife.
roots_lines: Hebrew et — a ploughshare or coulter; also the word in Isaiah 2:4, swords beaten into plowshares.
Hebrew charash — a worker in wood, stone or metal; 1 Samuel 13:19, “no smith found.”
Hebrew machareshah — a ploughshare; the companion tool in the same verse.
Hebrew maatsad — an axe or adze; another item on the list carried to the Philistines.
Latin culter, a knife or ploughshare — the source of the English word.
usage: “To sharpen every man his share, and his coulter” — farm tools sharpened at the enemy's forge.
“There was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel” — the disarmament stated plainly.
“Neither sword nor spear… but with Saul and with Jonathan” — two weapons in an army.

pos: v. (to fall in fine drops, as dew; Moses' word for the manner in which sound doctrine reaches a people)
etymology: From Latin destillare, to drop down, from de- and stilla, a drop. The Hebrew at Deuteronomy 32:2 is nazal, to flow or trickle; at Job 36:28 it is zalaph or nazal in the same sense of a fine falling moisture.
biblical_def: Moses opens his final song with a simile about teaching, and it is one of the most instructive verses in Scripture on how doctrine is to be delivered: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass” (Deuteronomy 32:2). Four images, and every one of them is gentle and gradual. Dew does not arrive; it forms. The small rain upon the tender herb is deliberately chosen — a downpour would flatten what the fine rain feeds. Moses had forty years of teaching a hard people behind him, and this is the figure he reached for. Elihu uses the word of the clouds: “Which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly” (Job 36:28), in a passage arguing from the ordinary works of God in the sky to His unsearchable greatness. Isaiah completes the doctrine by making the rain a figure of the word itself — it comes down, waters the earth, gives seed to the sower, and does not return void (Isaiah 55:10-11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines distil as to drop, to fall in drops, or to flow gently — and cites the Deuteronomy text.
webster_full: DISTIL, v.i. To drop; to fall in drops.
The dew that on the tender grass distils.
2. To flow gently, or in a small stream.
3. To use a still; to practice distillation.
DISTIL, v.t. To let fall in drops; to throw down in drops. My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew. Deut. 32.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 32:2
My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass:
Which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly.
Isaiah 55:10

For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater:
Deuteronomy 32:1
Give ear, O ye heavens, and I will speak; and hear, O earth, the words of my mouth.
corruption_summary: Teaching is measured by immediate visible effect, so the slow work Moses describes looks like failure and gets replaced by pressure.
corruption_paragraphs: Moses' simile is nearly the opposite of the modern instinct about communication. A ministry judged by measurable response will always prefer the downpour to the dew, because the downpour is visible and the dew is not, and the man whose speech distils will look ineffective beside the man who floods. Deuteronomy 32:2 does not disparage urgency — the same song contains some of the sharpest warnings in the Pentateuch — but it describes the ordinary manner of instruction as gradual, quiet, and cumulative, feeding the tender herb rather than flattening it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the corruption is one of method rather than meaning. The principle to recover is the patience of the sower and the promise attached to it. Isaiah 55 makes the rain a picture of the word precisely to guarantee the outcome: it shall not return void, it shall accomplish that which He pleases. That guarantee is what frees a preacher, a father, or a teacher from having to produce the harvest himself, and it is what makes years of unspectacular, dew-like teaching a reasonable use of a life. The dew that formed overnight did more for the herb than any storm.
roots_summary: Hebrew nazal, to flow or trickle — Deuteronomy 32:2; araph, to drop — the companion verb; tal, dew; Latin destillare, to fall in drops.
roots_lines: Hebrew nazal — to flow, trickle, distil; Deuteronomy 32:2 of Moses' speech.
Hebrew araph — to drip or drop; the parallel verb of the same verse, of doctrine as rain.
Hebrew tal — dew; the figure for what forms quietly and feeds.
Hebrew seir — the small rain upon the tender herb; deliberately distinguished from a downpour.
Latin destillare, from stilla, a drop — the source of the English word.
usage: “My speech shall distil as the dew” — Moses' own figure for teaching.
“The small rain upon the tender herb” — a downpour would flatten what this feeds.
“It shall not return unto me void” — the promise that makes slow sowing reasonable.

pos: n. (coarse broken flax or hemp fibre, notoriously quick to burn; the image of Samson's bonds snapping and of the strong man consumed by his own idol)
etymology: From Old English tow, spinning material, related to tools for working flax. The Hebrew at Isaiah 1:31 is neoreth, the shaken-out refuse of flax; at Judges 16:9 the phrase is pethil neoreth, a thread of tow.
biblical_def: Tow is the coarse fibre shaken out in the dressing of flax — the part fit for nothing but tinder. Judges uses it for the ease with which Samson broke his first bonds: “he brake the withs, as a thread of tow is broken when it toucheth the fire. So his strength was not known” (Judges 16:9). The comparison is exact and it is also a warning; a man who can snap green withs like burnt tinder was, three attempts later, shorn and blind and grinding at a mill. Isaiah turns the same material into a picture of judgment on idolaters: “And the strong shall be as tow, and the maker of it as a spark, and they shall both burn together, and none shall quench them” (Isaiah 1:31). The idol-maker and the idol go up in the same fire, and the fire is supplied by the man himself — he is the spark. Isaiah repeats the figure against the armies of Egypt: “they shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow” (Isaiah 43:17). What burns fastest is what looked strongest.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tow as the coarse and broken part of flax or hemp, separated from the finer part by the hatchel or swingle.
webster_full: TOW, n. The coarse and broken part of flax or hemp, separated from the finer part by the hatchel or swingle.
TOW, v.t. To drag, as a boat or ship, through the water by means of a rope.
FLAX, n. A plant of the genus Linum, consisting of a single slender stalk, the skin or herl of which is used for making thread and cloth.
HATCHEL, n. An instrument formed with long iron teeth set in a board, for cleaning flax or hemp.
TINDER, n. Something very inflammable, used for kindling fire from a spark.
scriptures: Judges 16:9

Now there were men lying in wait, abiding with her in the chamber. And she said unto him, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And he brake the withs, as a thread of tow is broken when it toucheth the fire. So his strength was not known.
Isaiah 1:31
And the strong shall be as tow, and the maker of it as a spark, and they shall both burn together, and none shall quench them.
Isaiah 43:17
Which bringeth forth the chariot and horse, the army and the power; they shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow.
Judges 16:20

And she said, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And he awoke out of his sleep, and said, I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself. And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.
corruption_summary: Samson is read as a folk-hero of raw strength, and the narrative's actual verdict — that his strength was never his — is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular treatment of Samson makes him a strongman whose secret was his hair, and the story becomes a fable about keeping a talisman. Judges says something else. The strength was the LORD's, the hair was the sign of a Nazarite vow, and the vow was the thing being broken piece by piece long before the razor came — the lion's carcase, the feasts, the women. The verse that names the tragedy is Judges 16:20: he wist not that the LORD was departed from him. He expected to shake himself as at other times, and his real loss had happened invisibly and by degrees. A man may break withs like tow for years and be nearly finished.

Isaiah 1:31 supplies the harder doctrine, and it is one the modern reader resists: the idolater supplies the fire that destroys him. The strong shall be as tow, and the maker of it as a spark. Judgment here is not an external penalty arbitrarily attached to sin but the working out of what sin is, so that the man and his idol burn together in a fire he struck. This does not make God passive — the same chapter is full of His active dealing — but it explains why Scripture so often describes the wicked as falling into the pit they dug. What looked like strength was tinder the whole time.
roots_summary: Hebrew neoreth, the refuse of flax, tow — Judges 16:9, Isaiah 1:31; pethil, a thread or cord — Judges 16:9; pishtah, flax — the material dressed.
roots_lines: Hebrew neoreth — tow, the coarse shaken-out part of flax; Judges 16:9 and Isaiah 1:31.

Hebrew nitsots — a spark; Isaiah 1:31, of the idol-maker himself.
Old English tow — spinning stuff; the source of the English noun.
usage: “As a thread of tow is broken when it toucheth the fire” — the ease of Samson's first escape.
“The strong shall be as tow, and the maker of it as a spark” — idol and idolater in one fire.
“He wist not that the LORD was departed from him” — the loss that happened invisibly.

pos: n. pl. (pliant twigs or cords of green willow, used as bonds; the first of Delilah's four attempts on Samson)
etymology: From Old English withthe, a willow twig, related to withy, the willow itself. The Hebrew is yether, a cord or bowstring — the margin of the Authorized Version notes the alternative rendering new cords, and the Hebrew adds lachim, moist or fresh.
biblical_def: Withs are green, unseasoned willow cords, and their strength is proverbial — a fresh withy binds where a dry one snaps. The word occurs three times, all in one episode. Samson tells Delilah: “If they bind me with seven green withs that were never dried, then shall I be weak, and be as another man” (Judges 16:7). She acts on it at once: “Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven green withs which had not been dried, and she bound him with them” (Judges 16:8). And the outcome: “he brake the withs, as a thread of tow is broken when it toucheth the fire. So his strength was not known” (Judges 16:9). The number seven and the specification never dried give the lie a ritual air, as though Samson were inventing a plausible superstition; but the reader should notice what the episode really discloses. Delilah had already told him plainly what she wanted — to know wherewith he might be bound to afflict him — and there were armed men in the room. He kept coming back. The withs failed; the pattern of returning to the thing that was hunting him did not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines with or withe as a twig or flexible branch, particularly of willow, used as a band or rope.
webster_full: WITHE, n. A willow twig; a flexible twig used as a band.
2. A band consisting of a twig, or of twigs twisted.
If they bind me with seven green withs. Judges 16.
WITHY, n. The willow, or a large species of willow.
BAND, n. A fillet; a cord; a tie; a chain; any narrow ligament with which a thing is bound.
scriptures: Judges 16:7
And Samson said unto her, If they bind me with seven green withs that were never dried, then shall I be weak, and be as another man.
Judges 16:8
Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven green withs which had not been dried, and she bound him with them.
Judges 16:9

Now there were men lying in wait, abiding with her in the chamber. And she said unto him, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And he brake the withs, as a thread of tow is broken when it toucheth the fire. So his strength was not known.
Proverbs 7:22
He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks;
corruption_summary: The episode is read as a story about a woman's deceit, when the narrative's weight falls on a man who saw the trap plainly and returned to it.
corruption_paragraphs: Retellings of Judges 16 concentrate on Delilah, and the moral drawn is generally a warning about treacherous women. That is not where the narrator puts the emphasis. Delilah's intention is stated openly in verse 6, before any of the four attempts, and the armed men are in the chamber. Samson is not deceived about her purpose at any point; he is simply unwilling to leave. This is the anatomy of besetting sin that Proverbs describes at length — the young man void of understanding going the way to her house, knowing the way and going it — and the Authorized Version's own comparison is a beast walking to the slaughter.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that knowledge is not deliverance. Samson could have written an accurate account of his danger and did in fact break every bond they tried, which only prolonged the arrangement and deepened the trust that he was invulnerable. The four attempts are recorded so that the reader watches a man survive three warnings and lose on the fourth. Whatever a man can break repeatedly, he will eventually stop being able to break; the withs held nothing, and the habit held everything.
roots_summary: Hebrew yether, a cord or bowstring — Judges 16:7-9; lach, moist or fresh — the green, undried quality; Old English withthe, a willow twig.
roots_lines: Hebrew yether — a cord, string, or bowstring; the word rendered withs in Judges 16.
Hebrew lach — moist, fresh, green; the specification that they were never dried.
Hebrew asar — to bind; the verb used of every attempt on Samson.
Hebrew shibah — seven; the number Samson specified, giving the lie a ritual sound.
Old English withthe, a willow twig, whence withy — the source of the English word.
usage: “Seven green withs that were never dried” — the first of four false answers.
“So his strength was not known” — and he stayed in the room.
The narrative's weight is on the man who returned, not the woman who asked.

pos: n. pl. (reeds or rushes growing in shallow water; the growth among which the ark of bulrushes was laid and found)
etymology: Middle English flagge, a reed or rush — unrelated to the banner sense of the word, which is later. The Hebrew at Exodus 2:3 is suph, reeds — the same word in yam suph, the Sea of Reeds, which the Authorized Version renders the Red sea.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word is suph, and the coincidence of vocabulary is worth pausing over. Moses was hidden as an infant “in the flags by the river's brink” (Exodus 2:3), and found there when “she saw the ark among the flags” (Exodus 2:5). Eighty years later he would lead Israel through the yam suph, the sea of the same reeds. The infant drawn out of the water among the flags becomes the man through whom a nation is drawn out of the water. Isaiah uses the plant as a measure of judgment on Egypt's whole economy: “the brooks of defence shall be emptied and dried up: the reeds and flags shall wither” (Isaiah 19:6) — when the Nile fails, the marsh growth on which so much Egyptian life depended fails first. Bildad draws a proverb from the same botany: “Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?” (Job 8:11). His application to Job is wrong and unkind, but the observation is sound and Scripture uses it elsewhere rightly — what has no root in water withers when the sun is up.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives flag as an aquatic plant, with long ensiform leaves, of several species — distinct from the banner sense of the word.
webster_full: FLAG, n. An aquatic plant, with a bladed leaf, of the genus Iris; also a species of Acorus.
The flags of the Nile, among which the ark of Moses was laid.
FLAG, n. A cloth, usually bearing a device, borne on a staff; an ensign; a colors.
RUSH, n. A plant of the genus Juncus, growing in wet or moist ground.
BULRUSH, n. A large kind of rush, growing in wet land or water.
scriptures: Exodus 2:3
And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink.
Exodus 2:5
And the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself at the river; and her maidens walked along by the river's side; and when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it.
Isaiah 19:6
And they shall turn the rivers far away; and the brooks of defence shall be emptied and dried up: the reeds and flags shall wither.
Job 8:11
Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?
corruption_summary: Exodus 2 is treated as a borrowed birth-legend, which removes the deliberate providence the narrative is constructed to display.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatments compare Exodus 2 to the Mesopotamian legend of Sargon, who was likewise set adrift in a reed basket, and conclude that the account of Moses is a literary borrowing meant to dignify a national founder. The parallel is real and proves nothing about historicity; exposed infants and river baskets were features of the ancient world, not of one story. What no parallel supplies is the structure Exodus builds: a decree that Hebrew sons be cast into the river, a mother who obeys the letter of it by placing her son in the river in a sealed ark, the daughter of the man who issued the decree drawing him out, and the child's own mother hired to nurse him at Pharaoh's expense. That is not legend-shape; it is providence-shape, and it is told with irony throughout.

The word ark in Exodus 2:3 is tebah, used elsewhere in Scripture only of Noah's ark — a vessel with no rudder, sealed with pitch, carrying the hope of a people through water that was killing everything else. The flags are the small physical detail that holds the whole scene together: they caught the ark, they kept it from the current, and they put it where Pharaoh's daughter would wash. Nothing in the account is presented as coincidence, and Hebrews 11 credits the parents' act to faith, adding that they were not afraid of the king's commandment.
roots_summary: Hebrew suph, reeds or flags — Exodus 2:3, 2:5; the same word in yam suph, the sea of reeds; achu, marsh grass — Job 8:11; tebah, ark — Exodus 2:3.
roots_lines: Hebrew suph — reeds, flags; Exodus 2:3 and 2:5, and the yam suph Israel crossed.
Hebrew tebah — an ark or chest; used in Scripture only of Noah's vessel and Moses' basket.
Hebrew gome — papyrus, bulrush; the material of the ark itself.
Hebrew achu — marsh grass, meadow; Job 8:11, and the reed-grass of Pharaoh's dream.
Middle English flagge — a reed; unrelated to the later banner sense of the word.
usage: “She laid it in the flags by the river's brink” — the reeds that held the ark from the current.
“When she saw the ark among the flags” — Pharaoh's daughter draws out Pharaoh's enemy.
“Can the flag grow without water?” — Bildad's sound botany and unsound application.

pos: n. pl. (clusters, chiefly of raisins; and once the humps of camels — the word for what is gathered and carried)
etymology: Middle English bunche, a lump or swelling, whence both the cluster sense and the hump sense. The Hebrew at 2 Samuel 16:1 is tsimmuqim, dried grapes; at Isaiah 30:6 it is dabbesheth, a hump.
biblical_def: The word gathers two quite different pictures. The first is provision brought to a king in flight. Ziba met David past the top of the hill “with a couple of asses saddled, and upon them two hundred loaves of bread, and an hundred bunches of raisins, and an hundred of summer fruits, and a bottle of wine” (2 Samuel 16:1) — a generosity whose motive the narrative later calls into serious question. The same commodity appears in a scene of unmixed joy when the tribes came to make David king: they “brought bread on asses, and on camels, and on mules, and on oxen, and meat, meal, cakes of figs, and bunches of raisins, and wine, and oil… for there was joy in Israel” (1 Chronicles 12:40). Dried grapes travelled well and kept, which is why they appear wherever Scripture describes provision for a journey. The second picture is a rebuke: Judah loading treasure for an Egyptian alliance, carrying “their treasures upon the bunches of camels, to a people that shall not profit them” (Isaiah 30:6). And the passover gives the smallest bunch of all — “a bunch of hyssop” dipped in blood (Exodus 12:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bunch as a protuberance or hunch, and also a cluster, a number of things of the same kind growing or fastened together.
webster_full: BUNCH, n. A protuberance; a hunch; a knob or lump; as the bunch on a camel's back.
2. A cluster; a number of the same kind growing together; as a bunch of grapes.
3. A number of things tied together; as a bunch of rods.
4. A collection of things; a knot.
RAISIN, n. A dried grape.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 16:1

And when David was a little past the top of the hill, behold, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of asses saddled, and upon them two hundred loaves of bread, and an hundred bunches of raisins, and an hundred of summer fruits, and a bottle of wine.
1 Chronicles 12:40

Moreover they that were nigh them, even unto Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, brought bread on asses, and on camels, and on mules, and on oxen, and meat, meal, cakes of figs, and bunches of raisins, and wine, and oil, and oxen, and sheep abundantly: for there was joy in Israel.
Isaiah 30:6

The burden of the beasts of the south: into the land of trouble and anguish, from whence come the young and old lion, the viper and fiery flying serpent, they will carry their riches upon the shoulders of young asses, and their treasures upon the bunches of camels, to a people that shall not profit them.
Exodus 12:22

And ye shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the bason, and strike the lintel and the two side posts with the blood that is in the bason; and none of you shall go out at the door of his house until the morning.
corruption_summary: Generosity is assumed to prove goodwill, and Ziba's laden asses are the standing scriptural warning that it does not.
corruption_paragraphs: Ziba arrives at the worst hour of David's life with exactly what a fleeing king needs, tells him that Mephibosheth has defected, and is rewarded with all his master's property. Mephibosheth's own account, given when David returns, is that Ziba slandered him and left him — a lame man who could not saddle an ass — unable to follow the king. Scripture does not adjudicate the case for us; David divides the land, and the reader is left with an unresolved question and a plain lesson. A gift arriving at the right moment is evidence of nothing but timing, and a generous man may be building a claim.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the corruption is the perennial one of buying influence. The principle to recover is the difference between the two scenes. In 1 Chronicles 12:40 the same raisins and figs are brought by tribes who had nothing to gain and are described as bringing them for there was joy in Israel. In 2 Samuel 16:1 they are brought by a servant who gains an estate that afternoon. The commodity is identical; the transaction is not. Churches receive both kinds of gift, and the difference is rarely visible in the moment of giving.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsimmuqim, dried grapes or raisins — 2 Samuel 16:1, 1 Chronicles 12:40; dabbesheth, a camel's hump — Isaiah 30:6; aguddah, a bunch or band — Exodus 12:22.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsimmuqim — raisins, dried grapes; 2 Samuel 16:1 and 1 Chronicles 12:40.
Hebrew dabbesheth — a hump; Isaiah 30:6, of camels loaded for Egypt.
Hebrew aguddah — a band, bunch, or bundle; Exodus 12:22, the bunch of hyssop.
Hebrew debelim — cakes of pressed figs; the companion travelling food.
Middle English bunche — a lump or swelling, whence both English senses.
usage: “An hundred bunches of raisins” — Ziba's well-timed generosity.
“For there was joy in Israel” — the same gift with a different motive.
“A bunch of hyssop” — the smallest bunch in Scripture, dipped in blood.

pos: n. pl. (the gut or sinew cords of a musical instrument, and of a bow; the psalter's instrument of ten strings and the archer's ready arrow)
etymology: From Old English streng, a cord or rope. The Hebrew at Psalm 33:2 is asor, a ten-stringed instrument; at Psalm 21:12 the word is yether, a bowstring — the same word rendered withs in Judges 16.
biblical_def: Three of the four occurrences name the same instrument. “Praise the LORD with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings” (Psalm 33:2); “Upon an instrument of ten strings, and upon the psaltery; upon the harp with a solemn sound” (Psalm 92:3); “I will sing a new song unto thee, O God: upon a psaltery and an instrument of ten strings will I sing praises unto thee” (Psalm 144:9). The Hebrew asor simply means a ten, and the psalms pair it with the psaltery and the harp as the ordinary furniture of temple praise. The fourth use is martial: “Therefore shalt thou make them turn their back, when thou shalt make ready thine arrows upon thy strings against the face of them” (Psalm 21:12). The same Hebrew word serves for a bowstring and for the green cords that failed to hold Samson — a cord under tension is a cord under tension, whether it sends an arrow or a note. Psalm 92:3 adds the phrase with a solemn sound, which in the Hebrew is higgaion, a meditative murmur; the temple string music was not entertainment but meditation given a voice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a string as a small rope or line, and particularly the cord of a musical instrument or of a bow.
webster_full: STRING, n. A small rope, line or cord, or a slender strip of leather or other like substance, used for fastening or tying things.
2. A ribin.
3. A thread on which any thing is filed.
4. The chord of a musical instrument, as of a harp or violin.
5. The line or cord of a bow, by which an arrow is impelled.
scriptures: Psalm 33:2
Praise the LORD with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings.
Psalm 92:3
Upon an instrument of ten strings, and upon the psaltery; upon the harp with a solemn sound.
Psalm 144:9
I will sing a new song unto thee, O God: upon a psaltery and an instrument of ten strings will I sing praises unto thee.
Psalm 21:12
Therefore shalt thou make them turn their back, when thou shalt make ready thine arrows upon thy strings against the face of them.
corruption_summary: These texts are enlisted on both sides of the instruments question, and the regulative principle is the point neither side should skip.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 33:2, 92:3, and 144:9 are quoted constantly in the debate over instruments in worship, and both parties tend to move too fast. The exclusive-psalmody and non-instrumental Reformed tradition observes correctly that these instruments belonged to the temple service, that the temple service is fulfilled and abolished in Christ, and that the New Testament nowhere commands instruments for the church. The other side observes correctly that the Psalms are the church's own hymnbook and that they command what they command. What both must submit to is the regulative principle itself: in corporate worship what Scripture commands is required, and what Scripture has not commanded is not permitted — which makes this a question about warrant and not about taste.

Whatever a congregation concludes on that question, Psalm 92:3 supplies a standard that has been largely lost. The string music of the temple was played with a solemn sound — Hebrew higgaion, a low meditative murmur, the same word appended to Psalm 9:16 alongside Selah. It was music arranged to help a man think, not to relieve him of thinking. Much contemporary church music is engineered for the opposite effect, and that criticism holds whichever side of the instruments question one takes. Praise directed to the God who is there ought to be as deliberate as the ten strings and as considered as the meditation they accompanied.
roots_summary: Hebrew asor, a ten-stringed instrument — Psalms 33:2, 92:3, 144:9; yether, a bowstring — Psalm 21:12; higgaion, a solemn meditative sound — Psalm 92:3.
roots_lines: Hebrew asor — literally “a ten”; the ten-stringed instrument of the psalms.
Hebrew nebel — the psaltery; the companion instrument in all three psalms.
Hebrew kinnor — the harp; David's own instrument before Saul.
Hebrew yether — a cord or bowstring; Psalm 21:12, and the withs of Judges 16:7.
Hebrew higgaion — a murmur, meditation; Psalm 92:3, “with a solemn sound.”
usage: “An instrument of ten strings” — the Hebrew is simply a ten.
“Upon the harp with a solemn sound” — music arranged to help a man think.
“Thine arrows upon thy strings” — the same Hebrew word for a bowstring.

pos: n. pl. (porters, carriers of loads; the seventy thousand of Solomon's levy, and the men whose strength Nehemiah reports as decayed)
etymology: From bear — Old English beran, to carry — with the agent ending. The Hebrew phrase in every occurrence is nose sabbal or sabbalim, bearers of burdens; the root sabal means to load or carry a heavy thing.
biblical_def: The bearers of burdens are the unnamed men whose labour stands behind every building project in Scripture. Solomon's levy: “he set threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work” (2 Chronicles 2:18). Josiah's repair of the house is organised the same way, with Levites “over the bearers of burdens… and overseers of all that wrought the work in any manner of service” (2 Chronicles 34:13). Then Nehemiah records the sentence that every man who has laboured a long time at a hard work recognises: “And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall” (Nehemiah 4:10). Three things at once — the workers are spent, the debris is greater than expected, and the conclusion drawn is that the work cannot be finished. It is the exact midpoint of the book, and it comes with the enemy massing outside. Nehemiah's answer was not a speech about morale but a redeployment: half at the work, half with weapons, and every builder with his sword girded.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bearer as one who bears, carries or conveys, and one who sustains or supports.
webster_full: BEARER, n. One who bears, sustains, or carries; a carrier, especially of a corpse to the grave.
2. One who wears any thing; as the bearer of a sword.
3. A tree or plant that yields its fruit; as a good bearer.
BEAR, v.t. To support; to sustain; as, to bear a weight or burden.
BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 2:18
And he set threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work.
2 Chronicles 34:13
Also they were over the bearers of burdens, and were overseers of all that wrought the work in any manner of service: and of the Levites there were scribes, and officers, and porters.
Nehemiah 4:10
And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall.
Galatians 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
corruption_summary: Ministry exhaustion is treated as a personal failure of resilience, when Nehemiah 4:10 records it as a corporate and structural condition.
corruption_paragraphs: When workers give out, the modern instinct is to address the worker — his habits, his boundaries, his capacity. Nehemiah 4:10 does not read that way. The report is corporate (Judah said), the causes are external as well as internal (strength decayed and much rubbish), and the conclusion reached is doctrinal despair (we are not able). Nehemiah responds to all three. He does not deny the fatigue, he does not lecture the men, and he does not simply exhort them to try harder; he reorganises the work so that half stand guard while half build, and he sets families together at the portion of wall nearest their own houses. The remedy is structural, and it is also spiritual: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture names the labourers. Seventy thousand bearers of burdens are recorded in the account of Solomon's temple, and not one of them is named individually; the Chronicler counted them anyway. Every visible work rests on invisible carrying, and Paul makes the same carrying a law of the church: bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. Where that command is obeyed, the strength of the bearers is renewed by distribution rather than exhortation, which is precisely what Nehemiah did with a trowel in one hand and a weapon in the other.
roots_summary: Hebrew sabbal, a burden-bearer — 2 Chronicles 2:18, Nehemiah 4:10; sabal, to bear a load; massa, a burden; Greek baros, weight — Galatians 6:2.
roots_lines: Hebrew sabbal — a burden-bearer, porter; 2 Chronicles 2:18 and Nehemiah 4:10.
Hebrew sabal — to carry a heavy load; the verb used of the Servant bearing iniquities in Isaiah 53:11.
Hebrew massa — a burden, and also an oracle or prophetic weight.
Hebrew koach — strength; Nehemiah 4:10, “the strength of the bearers… is decayed.”
Greek baros — weight, burden; Galatians 6:2, the burdens the church is to carry for one another.
usage: “Threescore and ten thousand… bearers of burdens” — counted though unnamed.
“The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish” — fatigue and debris together.
“Bear ye one another's burdens” — the same carrying made a law of the church.
